## Overview

R and C++ errors leave a function differently:

- A C++ exception walks back through C++ code and runs destructors.
- An R error jumps directly back to R. C++ destructors in its path do not run.

An R error is always possible when calling R. Allocation can fail, an interrupt can arrive, and a warning becomes an error under `options(warn = 2)`.

At the interface between packages, `charport` therefore normalizes on R's `Rf_error()`/long-jump system. This is the one error system every R package shares, without requiring Rcpp, cpp11, or another C++ framework.

Inside C++ code, `charport` temporarily turns that R jump into a C++ exception. Destructors run, and the original R error then continues. Rcpp and cpp11 perform this bridge differently, which is why `charport` selects a compile-time adapter for each entry style.

The reverse direction is simpler: a C++ exception must not leave through a C entry point. The outer boundary lets C++ cleanup finish before reporting an R error on the main thread.

## C++ framework determines error handling

`Rcpp` and `cpp11` handle R errors differently. Therefore, the presence of the `Rcpp.h` or `cpp11.hpp` selects a corresponding compile-time adapter that changes how error handling is processed (see `inst/include/interop/unwind.h`). The usage is summarized as follows:

| R enters through | Include order | Outer error boundary |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| Hand-written `.Call` | `charport.h` | `charport::r_boundary()` |
| Rcpp generated wrapper | `Rcpp.h`, then `charport.h` | Generated by Rcpp |
| cpp11 generated wrapper | `cpp11.hpp`, then `charport.h` | Generated by cpp11 |

Within `Reader` and `charvec::Builder` (and variants) wrapping uses the selected adapter internally. The interface use is the same in all three cases:

``` cpp
charport::Reader input(x);
charport::charvec::Builder output(input.size());

for(R_xlen_t i = 0; i < input.size(); ++i) {
  output.set(i, input[i]);
}

return output.to_sexp();
```

### Hand-Written `.Call`

A hand-written entry point supplies its own outer boundary:

``` cpp
#include "charport.h"

extern "C" SEXP C_copy(SEXP x) {
  return charport::r_boundary("copy", [&]() -> SEXP {
    charport::Reader input(x);
    charport::charvec::Builder output(input.size());
    for(R_xlen_t i = 0; i < input.size(); ++i) {
      output.set(i, input[i]);
    }
    return output.to_sexp();
  });
}
```

Place the boundary before any C++ objects whose cleanup matters. For an additional raw R call, protect only that call:

``` cpp
return charport::unwind_protect([&]() -> SEXP {
  return Rf_eval(expression, environment);
});
```

### Foreign Error-Handler Macros

A package that already has its own error-handler macro system (outside of `Rcpp` or `cpp11`) can integrate charport's standalone backend at that boundary. Catch `charport::r_unwind`, record its token, and leave the catch block before continuing the R unwind:

``` cpp
SEXP unwind_token = R_NilValue;
try {
  charport::Reader input(x);
  // ...
} catch(const charport::r_unwind& error) {
  cleanup();
  unwind_token = error.token;
}

if(unwind_token != R_NilValue) {
  charport::continue_r_unwind(unwind_token);
}
```

Do not call `R_ContinueUnwind()` or otherwise long-jump from inside the live catch block: doing so skips destruction of the in-flight C++ exception object. The standalone token is preserved separately for each throw, and `continue_r_unwind()` releases it before resuming the original R condition.

## Provider Initialization

`init(SEXP)` may return `NULL` to decline a vector. Its error convention is `Rf_error()` only; any possible C++ exceptions are caught within the callback.

If initialization needs both R-facing work and C++ state, do the R work first. Once C++ state exists, an R error would jump over its destructors.

Range and indexed callbacks must not call R or throw. Release callbacks have no error channel.

## Worker Threads

`Reader` construction, `Builder::to_sexp()` and anything else involving the R API should stay on the main thread. `Reader` access on worker threads should only be done when `Reader::concurrent_access()` is true.
